title: I’m In. Here’s the (Start of the) Plan.
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart recounts turning down a lucrative business-partner opportunity years earlier to keep teaching, and revisits that choice mid-pandemic while proctoring an AP exam. He affirms he'd make the same choice again -- not from guilt or a savior complex, but because he still believes teaching is good and schools remain the places with the greatest potential for advancing children's long-term flourishing. He pivots from personal reaffirmation to a public commitment: over the coming weeks he will publish a series on the few emphases he believes deserve priority as schools plan for the next year. He closes with a structural claim that anchors the coming series -- that the system to be improved is people, not policies, and that lip service without heart-level change 'only deepens our dysphoria.'
points: Stuart frames his decision to keep teaching as a renewed, non-guilt-based choice made mid-pandemic, contrasting it with a specific declined opportunity (a business partnership) to make the stakes concrete.
He explicitly rejects the 'savior' framing of staying in teaching, naming instead a belief that teaching and learning remain uniquely potential-laden work.

His structural thesis for the piece: 'the system we aim to improve isn't policies and procedures — it's people' -- meaning top-down PD or policy change without heart-level buy-in from teachers doesn't produce durable change.
The article functions as a public commitment device, announcing an upcoming series on the priorities he believes should guide planning for the next school year.
quotes: There was just one problem: I'd have to be done teaching and writing. After all, I'm not willing to work around the clock and sacrifice my family for success.
There is just something about this job — remote or in-person, masked or not, grading or teaching, connecting or troubleshooting — that feels like home.

No. It's just that I still think teaching is good. I think learning is beautiful. I think schools are still the places with the greatest potential for advancing the long-term flourishing of each child.

The system we aim to improve isn't policies and procedures — it's people. It's not what's said a few times during a single day of PD — it's what's said a thousand times in the hearts and minds and mouths of the folks who work within the system.
Changing things on paper without changing things in the hearts and minds of teachers doesn't do much. Lip service is an illusion; it only deepens our dysphoria.
None of what I just said is easy. But it's reality. There are no better partners than reality.
